q: The branch of biology that studies the chemical components of living things and the reactions they undergo is called:
x: Biochemistry deals with the chemistry of life: the molecules of cells and their reactions. Physiology studies the functions of organs and systems, not their chemistry as such.

q: By mass, the most abundant element in protoplasm is:
x: Oxygen makes up about 65% of protoplasm by mass, mainly because cells are mostly water. Carbon comes second at about 18%.

q: Which of the following molecules in a cell has the largest molecular mass?
x: A chromosome's DNA is a single enormous polymer of millions of nucleotides. Haemoglobin is a macromolecule too, but far smaller; sucrose and glucose are small molecules.

q: Which group of four elements together makes up about 96% of the mass of living matter?
x: Oxygen (about 65%), carbon (18%), hydrogen (10%) and nitrogen (3%) add up to about 96%. Calcium and phosphorus are next but are present in much smaller amounts.

q: The most abundant compound in a living cell is:
x: Water makes up about 70% or more of a cell's mass. Proteins are the most abundant organic compounds, but water is the most abundant compound overall.

q: Which class of organic compounds makes up the largest share of the dry mass of most cells?
x: Proteins form more than half of the dry mass of a typical cell. Carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids each make up a smaller share.

q: Organic compounds are those that:
o: Are made only inside living organisms
Contain carbon atoms bonded to hydrogen
x: Organic compounds have a carbon skeleton bonded to hydrogen. Many can be made in a laboratory, many contain no nitrogen, and lipids do not dissolve in water.

q: Which of the following is an inorganic substance found in cells?
x: Potassium chloride is a mineral salt with no carbon–hydrogen skeleton, so it is inorganic. Urea, glycerol and ribose are all organic carbon compounds.

q: Carbon forms the backbone of biological molecules mainly because a carbon atom:
o: Is the most abundant element in protoplasm
Readily forms ionic bonds with metals
Can form four covalent bonds, including bonds with other carbon atoms
Has the largest atomic mass among bioelements
x: Carbon is tetravalent and can bond to other carbon atoms, forming chains, branches and rings. This gives the huge variety of organic molecules. Oxygen, not carbon, is the most abundant element by mass.

q: Biological molecules are divided into micromolecules and macromolecules. Which group consists ONLY of micromolecules?
o: Glucose, amino acids and fatty acids
x: Glucose, amino acids and fatty acids are small molecules (monomers or building blocks). Starch, DNA, proteins, cellulose and glycogen are macromolecules.

q: The monomers from which proteins are built are:
x: Proteins are polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. Nucleotides build nucleic acids and monosaccharides build polysaccharides.

q: Nucleic acids are polymers of:
x: The monomer of DNA and RNA is the nucleotide: a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base and a phosphate group. A nucleoside lacks the phosphate.

q: Which pairing of a bond with the units it links is correct?
o: Glycosidic bond – fatty acids and glycerol
x: Peptide bonds join amino acids. Glycosidic bonds join monosaccharides, ester bonds join fatty acids to glycerol, and phosphodiester bonds join nucleotides.

q: Which of the following polymers is built from more than one kind of monomer?
x: A protein is made from about 20 different kinds of amino acids. Cellulose, starch and glycogen are all built from only one monomer, glucose.

q: Macromolecules are formed when:
o: Large molecules are broken by hydrolysis
Mineral ions combine by ionic bonding
Many small subunits are joined by condensation reactions
Water molecules link by hydrogen bonds
x: Macromolecules are polymers made by joining many monomers, each link formed by condensation (removal of water). Hydrolysis does the reverse.

q: The joining of two monomers with the removal of a water molecule is called:
x: In condensation, an –OH from one unit and an –H from the other are removed as water, and a bond forms between the units. Hydrolysis is the reverse, using water to break the bond.

q: During digestion, an enzyme splits one maltose molecule into two glucose molecules. This reaction is:
x: Breaking a glycosidic bond requires adding a water molecule, which is hydrolysis. Condensation is the reverse reaction, which releases water.

q: How many water molecules are released when 50 amino acids join to form a single unbranched polypeptide chain?
x: Each peptide bond releases one water molecule, and a chain of 50 amino acids has 49 peptide bonds. So 49 water molecules are released.

q: Complete hydrolysis of an unbranched polysaccharide chain of 200 glucose units into free glucose uses how many water molecules?
x: A chain of 200 units has 199 glycosidic bonds, and hydrolysis of each bond uses one water molecule, so 199 water molecules are needed.

q: Condensation reactions that build macromolecules from monomers are:
x: Building large molecules from small ones is anabolism, which needs an input of energy. Breaking them down (catabolism, for example hydrolysis) releases energy.

q: Metabolism is:
o: Only the breakdown of food molecules to release energy
Only the synthesis of large molecules from small ones
Only the reactions of respiration in mitochondria
The sum of all chemical reactions taking place in a cell or organism
x: Metabolism includes both anabolism (synthesis) and catabolism (breakdown). Respiration is just one part of catabolism.

q: Which element is present in all proteins but absent from glucose, starch and cellulose?
x: Every amino acid has an amino group, so all proteins contain nitrogen. Glucose, starch and cellulose contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

q: Phosphorus is an essential element of:
x: Each nucleotide of DNA and RNA has a phosphate group, so nucleic acids contain phosphorus. Cellulose, starch and triglycerides contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

q: Sulphur in proteins comes from amino acids such as:
x: Cysteine and methionine contain sulphur; cysteine can form disulphide bridges that help hold a protein's shape. The other amino acids listed contain no sulphur.

q: Which shows the four most abundant elements of protoplasm by mass, in order from highest to lowest?
x: By mass, oxygen is about 65%, carbon 18%, hydrogen 10% and nitrogen 3%. Hydrogen has the most atoms, but each atom is very light, so it ranks third by mass.

q: A compound from a cell contains C, H, O, N and P. On complete hydrolysis it gives a pentose sugar, nitrogenous bases and phosphate. It belongs to the class:
x: Pentose + nitrogenous base + phosphate are the parts of nucleotides, so the compound is a nucleic acid. A phospholipid also contains P but gives glycerol and fatty acids, not a pentose.

q: A sweet, crystalline compound has the formula C12H22O11. It belongs to the class:
x: C12H22O11 is the formula of a disaccharide such as sucrose or maltose: two hexoses (C6H12O6 each) minus one water. Monosaccharides are C6H12O6 or smaller.

q: Lipids are placed in one group mainly because they:
o: Are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents such as ether and chloroform
x: Lipids are a varied group defined by solubility: insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents. Only some (phospholipids) contain phosphorus.

q: The molecular mass of biological molecules is usually expressed in:
x: One dalton is about the mass of one hydrogen atom; molecular masses are given in daltons. Calories and joules measure energy, angstroms measure length.

q: Which list correctly gives the four main classes of organic biological molecules?
o: Nucleic acids, hormones, enzymes and water
Carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids
x: The four main classes of organic molecules in cells are carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. Water and mineral salts are inorganic.

q: Which statement about condensation and hydrolysis is correct?
o: Condensation adds water to a molecule, and hydrolysis removes it
Both are catalysed by enzymes, and hydrolysis uses one water molecule for each bond broken
Hydrolysis builds polymers, and condensation breaks them down
Condensation breaks glycosidic bonds, and hydrolysis forms them
x: In cells both reactions are enzyme-controlled. Condensation removes water to form a bond; hydrolysis adds one water molecule for each bond it breaks.

q: Which elements are needed by organisms only in very small (trace) amounts?
x: Copper, zinc and manganese are trace elements, often needed as parts of enzymes. Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and phosphorus are major elements present in large amounts.

q: The main and immediate source of energy for most cells is:
x: Glucose is broken down in respiration to release energy, which is trapped in ATP. Cellulose is structural, cholesterol is a membrane lipid and keratin is a structural protein.

q: Gram for gram, which class of compounds releases about twice as much energy as carbohydrates when oxidised?
x: Fats yield roughly twice the energy per gram of carbohydrates because they are richer in C–H bonds. Proteins yield about the same as carbohydrates.

q: Most enzymes, the biological catalysts of cells, are chemically:
x: Nearly all enzymes are globular proteins whose shape forms an active site. Lipids, polysaccharides and steroids do not act as enzymes.

q: Haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in red blood cells, is a:
x: Haemoglobin is a protein made of four polypeptide chains, each with an iron-containing haem group that binds oxygen.

q: Antibodies, which defend the body against foreign antigens, are:
x: Antibodies (immunoglobulins) are proteins made by B lymphocytes (plasma cells). Their specific shape lets them bind particular antigens.

q: In animal cells, cholesterol is important as:
o: The main structural material of the cell wall
The main source of immediate energy
A component of cell membranes and the starting material for steroid hormones
x: Cholesterol is a lipid that sits in animal cell membranes and is converted into steroid hormones such as testosterone and oestrogen. Animal cells have no cell wall.

q: Which pair correctly matches a hormone with its chemical nature?
x: Insulin and glucagon are protein (polypeptide) hormones. Testosterone and oestrogen are steroids, which are lipids derived from cholesterol.

q: In most organisms, hereditary information is stored in:
x: DNA carries the genes passed from parents to offspring. Glycogen is a stored carbohydrate, phospholipids build membranes and haemoglobin carries oxygen.

q: ATP, the energy currency of the cell, is chemically a:
x: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is a nucleotide: adenine, the sugar ribose and three phosphate groups. Energy is released when its terminal phosphate is removed.

q: The basic framework of all cell membranes is formed by a double layer of:
x: Membranes are built on a phospholipid bilayer with hydrophilic heads facing outwards and hydrophobic tails inwards. Cellulose forms plant cell walls, not membranes.

q: The layer of fat under the skin of mammals is important because it:
o: Insulates the body and stores energy
x: Subcutaneous fat is a poor conductor of heat, so it reduces heat loss, and it is a long-term energy store. It also cushions organs.

q: The waxy layer on the surface of leaves and fruits mainly:
x: Waxes are water-repellent lipids. On leaf and fruit surfaces they form a waterproof layer that cuts down evaporation.

q: Keratin, found in hair, nails, horns and feathers, is an example of a:
x: Keratin is a tough fibrous protein that gives strength to hair, nails and similar structures. It does not store energy or catalyse reactions.

q: Which protein gives strength to tendons, skin and the matrix of bone?
x: Collagen is a fibrous protein with high tensile strength, abundant in connective tissues. Myosin is a contractile protein of muscle.

q: Muscle contraction depends mainly on which two proteins?
x: Actin and myosin filaments slide over each other to shorten a muscle fibre. Keratin and collagen are structural, and insulin and glucagon are hormones.

q: In animals, excess glucose is stored as glycogen mainly in the:
x: Liver and muscle cells store glycogen. Liver glycogen is broken down to keep blood glucose steady; muscle glycogen fuels the muscle itself.

q: Plants store glucose as starch rather than as free glucose mainly because starch:
o: Diffuses quickly to all parts of the plant
Releases more energy per gram than fat
Is insoluble, so it does not raise the osmotic concentration of the cell
x: Large amounts of dissolved glucose would draw water into cells by osmosis. Starch is insoluble and osmotically inactive. Fat, not starch, releases more energy per gram.

q: Many animals store long-term energy as fat rather than glycogen. The main advantage of fat is that it:
o: Stores about twice as much energy per gram and is stored with little water
Can be broken down faster than glycogen
x: Fat holds about twice the energy per gram and is stored nearly water-free, so it is a compact reserve. Glycogen, however, is mobilised faster when quick energy is needed.

q: The body uses proteins as a major energy source mainly when:
o: Blood glucose is high just after a meal
Quick energy is needed for a short sprint
Carbohydrate and fat reserves are used up, as in prolonged starvation
x: Carbohydrates and fats are the normal fuels. Proteins are broken down for energy in large amounts only when those reserves run out.

q: Blood clotting depends on the conversion of which plasma protein into insoluble fibrin threads?
x: Soluble fibrinogen in plasma is converted into insoluble fibrin, which forms the mesh of a clot. Albumin is another plasma protein but it is not converted into fibrin.

q: Which mineral element is part of haemoglobin and essential for oxygen transport?
x: Each haem group of haemoglobin contains an iron (Fe²⁺) ion that binds oxygen. Lack of iron reduces haemoglobin and causes anaemia.

q: Magnesium is important to green plants because it is a component of:
x: A magnesium ion lies at the centre of each chlorophyll molecule. Cellulose and starch contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

q: Iodine is needed in the human body for making:
x: Iodine is part of the thyroid hormone thyroxine. Insulin, haemoglobin and keratin are proteins that do not need iodine.

q: Calcium ions in the human body are needed for:
o: Carrying oxygen in red blood cells
Forming the haem group of haemoglobin
Making thyroxine in the thyroid gland
Bone formation, muscle contraction and blood clotting
x: Calcium is a major part of bones and teeth and is needed for muscle contraction and blood clotting. Oxygen transport and haem depend on iron; thyroxine needs iodine.

q: Which carbohydrate is the main structural component of plant cell walls?
x: Cellulose fibres give plant cell walls their strength. Starch and glycogen are storage carbohydrates, and chitin is found in fungal walls and arthropod exoskeletons.

q: The tough exoskeleton of insects and crabs is made mainly of:
x: Arthropod exoskeletons are made of the polysaccharide chitin. Cellulose is in plant walls; keratin and collagen are animal structural proteins.

q: Ribose and deoxyribose are important to cells because they:
o: Are the main storage carbohydrates of the liver
Are the sugar parts of the nucleotides of RNA and DNA
Form the walls of plant cells
Are the main transport sugars in phloem
x: Ribose is the sugar of RNA nucleotides and deoxyribose that of DNA nucleotides. Glycogen is the liver store, cellulose builds walls and sucrose is the phloem sugar.

q: Oils stored in seeds such as sunflower and mustard serve mainly as:
o: The genetic material of the embryo
An energy reserve for the germinating seedling
x: Seed oils are triglycerides that the seedling oxidises for energy until it can photosynthesise. They are not enzymes or genetic material.

q: When a desert animal oxidises its stored fat, besides energy it also obtains:
x: Oxidation of fat produces carbon dioxide and water, and fat yields a lot of this metabolic water per gram. Fat contains no nitrogen or calcium, and its oxidation uses oxygen rather than supplying it.

q: Which protein stores oxygen inside muscle cells?
x: Myoglobin holds a reserve of oxygen in muscle. Haemoglobin carries oxygen in the blood, while myosin and actin are contractile proteins.

q: A student matches biological molecules with their functions. Which pairing is INCORRECT?
o: Cellulose – main energy store in animals
x: Cellulose is a structural carbohydrate of plant cell walls; animals store energy as glycogen and fat. The other three pairings are correct.

q: About what proportion of the mass of a typical living cell is water?
x: Water makes up roughly 70–90% of protoplasm, depending on the cell. A few organisms such as jellyfish have more, and some tissues such as bone have less.

q: A water molecule is polar because:
o: Hydrogen is more electronegative than oxygen
The atoms are held together by ionic bonds
The molecule is straight, with hydrogen atoms on opposite sides
Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen and pulls the shared electrons towards itself
x: Oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly, so it carries a partial negative charge and each hydrogen a partial positive charge. The molecule is bent, which keeps these charges unbalanced.

q: The angle between the two O–H bonds in a water molecule is about:
x: Water is a bent molecule with a bond angle of about 104.5°. If it were straight (180°), the partial charges would cancel and the molecule would not be polar.

q: Neighbouring water molecules are attracted to one another by:
x: The partially positive hydrogen of one water molecule is attracted to the partially negative oxygen of another, forming a hydrogen bond.

q: The bonds that hold the hydrogen and oxygen atoms together within a single water molecule are:
x: Within the molecule, O and H share electrons unequally, so the bonds are polar covalent. Hydrogen bonds are the weaker attractions between separate water molecules.

q: A hydrogen bond between two water molecules forms between:
o: A hydrogen atom of one molecule and the oxygen atom of another
The oxygen atoms of the two molecules
The hydrogen atoms of the two molecules
The two hydrogen atoms within the same molecule
x: Opposite partial charges attract: slightly positive hydrogen to slightly negative oxygen of a neighbouring molecule. Like charges (O–O or H–H) repel.

q: A single water molecule can form hydrogen bonds with at most how many neighbouring water molecules?
x: Each water molecule can form two hydrogen bonds through its hydrogen atoms and two through the lone pairs on its oxygen, making four. In ice, every molecule is bonded to four others.

q: When sodium chloride dissolves in water, each Na⁺ ion becomes surrounded by water molecules arranged with:
o: Their hydrogen atoms facing the ion
Their oxygen atoms facing the ion
x: The positive Na⁺ attracts the partially negative oxygen ends of water molecules. Cl⁻ ions, in contrast, are surrounded by the partially positive hydrogen ends.

q: Water is an excellent solvent in cells mainly because:
o: It has a low specific heat
It ionizes completely into H⁺ and OH⁻
Its polarity lets it dissolve ionic and polar substances
x: Polar water molecules surround ions and polar molecules and separate them, so salts, sugars and amino acids dissolve. Water ionizes only very slightly.

q: Oils and fats do not dissolve in water because their molecules are:
o: Too small to be surrounded by water
x: Non-polar molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds or ionic attractions with water, so water does not dissolve them. Polar and ionic substances are the ones that do dissolve.

q: Substances such as glucose and mineral salts, which dissolve readily in water, are described as:
x: Hydrophilic means 'water-loving': polar or charged substances that attract water molecules and dissolve. Hydrophobic, lipophilic and non-polar substances do not dissolve in water.

q: In which of the following does water act as a reagent (a reactant), not just as a solvent?
o: Cooling of the body by sweating
Floating of ice on a lake
x: In hydrolysis, water molecules are actually used up to break bonds, so water is a reactant. Dissolving, sweating and floating ice involve water's physical properties only.

q: In photosynthesis, water acts as a reagent because it:
o: Is the source of the carbon in glucose
Is split to supply hydrogen (electrons), releasing oxygen
Is the pigment that absorbs light
x: Water is split (photolysis) in the light reactions, providing hydrogen and electrons; its oxygen is released as O₂. The carbon in glucose comes from carbon dioxide.

q: Specific heat is the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1 °C. For water this is about:
x: Water's specific heat is about 1 calorie per gram per °C, which is high compared with most substances. Around 540 calories per gram is its heat of vaporisation, a different property.

q: Water has a high specific heat because:
o: Much of the heat absorbed is used to break hydrogen bonds before the molecules move faster
Its covalent O–H bonds break easily on heating
x: Heat first goes into breaking hydrogen bonds between molecules, so the temperature rises only slowly. The covalent O–H bonds are strong and do not break on ordinary heating.

q: A biological consequence of water's high specific heat is that:
o: Ice floats on the surface of lakes
Water rises in the xylem of tall trees
Salts dissolve easily in body fluids
Body temperature and the temperature of lakes and seas change only slowly
x: Water absorbs or loses a lot of heat with little temperature change, so organisms and aquatic habitats have stable temperatures. Floating ice is due to density, and rise in xylem to cohesion.

q: Sweating cools the body mainly because water has a high:
x: Evaporation of water needs a large amount of heat, which is taken from the skin. So even a little evaporating sweat removes much body heat.

q: Water's high specific heat and its high heat of vaporisation both result from:
x: Extra energy is needed to break the many hydrogen bonds between water molecules, both when warming water and when evaporating it.

q: Liquid water has its maximum density at about:
x: Water is densest at about 4 °C. Below this it expands as hydrogen bonds begin to form the open structure of ice.

q: Ice floats on liquid water because:
o: Its molecules are packed more closely than in liquid water
It contains dissolved salts that make it lighter
Hydrogen bonds hold its molecules further apart in an open lattice, so it is less dense
Its molecules have a lower molecular mass
x: In ice, each molecule is hydrogen-bonded to four others in a regular open lattice, which takes more space than liquid water. So ice is less dense and floats.

q: In winter the surface of a pond freezes, yet fish survive in the water below. This is mainly because:
o: The floating ice insulates the water beneath, which stays liquid at about 4 °C near the bottom
Ice is denser than water, so it sinks and leaves warm water on top
The pond freezes from the bottom upwards
Hydrogen bonds break when water freezes, releasing heat to the fish
x: Ice is less dense, so it forms a floating layer that insulates the water below. The densest water, at about 4 °C, sinks to the bottom and stays liquid. Hydrogen bonds form, not break, on freezing.

q: The attraction of water molecules to one another is called:
x: Cohesion is attraction between like molecules, here water to water through hydrogen bonds. Adhesion is attraction of water to other surfaces.

q: Cohesion of water molecules is important in plants because it:
o: Allows minerals to dissolve in soil water
Keeps the water column in the xylem unbroken as water is pulled up to the leaves
Provides the hydrogen used in photosynthesis
x: Hydrogen bonds hold water molecules together, so transpiration pull at the leaves draws up a continuous column through the xylem. Photosynthesis uses water as a reagent, not because of cohesion.

q: Water rises in a narrow glass tube partly because of adhesion. Adhesion is the attraction between:
o: Water molecules and the walls of the tube
Hydrogen and oxygen atoms within one molecule
x: Adhesion is attraction between water and a different substance, such as glass or xylem walls. Attraction between water molecules themselves is cohesion.

q: A pond skater (an insect) can walk on the surface of water because of water's:
o: High surface tension, due to cohesion
x: Hydrogen-bonded molecules at the surface pull inwards and together, giving a 'skin' with high surface tension that can support small insects.

q: The slight ionization of water is correctly shown as:
x: A very small fraction of water molecules dissociates reversibly into hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions. Water does not split into gases or peroxide in this way.

q: In pure water, the concentration of hydrogen ions is about 10⁻⁷ mol/L. What is the concentration of hydroxide ions?
x: Each water molecule that ionizes gives one H⁺ and one OH⁻, so in pure water their concentrations are equal: both about 10⁻⁷ mol/L, which gives pH 7.

q: In water, a hydrogen ion released by ionization quickly joins a water molecule to form a:
x: A free H⁺ (a proton) attaches to a water molecule, forming H₃O⁺. The hydroxide ion is the other product of ionization.

q: Pure water is neutral because:
o: It contains no ions at all
It contains more OH⁻ than H⁺ ions
It contains equal concentrations of H⁺ and OH⁻ ions
x: Water does ionize slightly, but always into equal numbers of H⁺ and OH⁻ ions, so neither acidity nor alkalinity dominates.

q: Which of the following is NOT a result of hydrogen bonding between water molecules?
o: The high surface tension of water
Ice being less dense than liquid water
The bonding of hydrogen to oxygen within each molecule
The high heat of vaporisation of water
x: Hydrogen and oxygen within a molecule are joined by polar covalent bonds, not hydrogen bonds. Surface tension, low density of ice and high heat of vaporisation all depend on hydrogen bonds between molecules.

q: Blood plasma carries glucose, urea and mineral ions around the body. This depends mainly on water's:
x: Because water dissolves polar and ionic substances, it acts as a transport medium in blood, lymph and xylem sap.

q: Water is a liquid at room temperature, while hydrogen sulphide (H₂S), a similar but heavier molecule, is a gas. This is because water:
o: Has a larger molecular mass than H₂S
Forms many hydrogen bonds between its molecules
Has ionic bonds between hydrogen and oxygen
x: Hydrogen bonds hold water molecules together, so much more energy is needed to turn water into vapour. Water is actually lighter than H₂S, and its O–H bonds are covalent, not ionic.

q: Chemically, carbohydrates are best described as:
o: Esters of fatty acids and glycerol
Polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or substances that yield them on hydrolysis
x: Carbohydrates carry several –OH groups plus an aldehyde or ketone group, or are polymers that break down to such sugars. Fats are esters, proteins are amino acid polymers.

q: The general formula of carbohydrates is:
x: Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with H and O usually in the 2:1 ratio of water, hence 'hydrates of carbon', Cx(H₂O)y.

q: A monosaccharide with six carbon atoms and an aldehyde group is called an:
x: 'Aldo-' means an aldehyde group and '-hexose' six carbons; glucose and galactose are aldohexoses. Fructose, with a ketone group, is a ketohexose.

q: Glucose and fructose have the same formula but differ in that:
o: Glucose has an aldehyde group while fructose has a ketone group
Glucose has five carbon atoms while fructose has six
Glucose is a disaccharide while fructose is a monosaccharide
Glucose contains nitrogen while fructose does not
x: Both are hexoses, C6H12O6. Glucose is an aldose (aldehyde group at carbon 1) and fructose a ketose (ketone group at carbon 2).

q: The simplest monosaccharides, the trioses, include:
x: Trioses have three carbons: glyceraldehyde (an aldose) and dihydroxyacetone (a ketose). Ribose, deoxyribose and ribulose are pentoses; glucose, galactose and fructose are hexoses.

q: Monosaccharides contain:
x: Monosaccharides range from trioses (3 C) to heptoses (7 C). The most common are pentoses and hexoses.

q: Deoxyribose, the sugar of DNA, differs from ribose in having:
o: A ketone group instead of an aldehyde group
One oxygen atom fewer (C5H10O4 instead of C5H10O5)
Six carbon atoms instead of five
x: 'Deoxy' means lacking an oxygen: at carbon 2, deoxyribose has –H instead of –OH. Both are five-carbon sugars.

q: Which pentose, in its phosphorylated form, accepts carbon dioxide in photosynthesis?
x: Ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP), a ketopentose, combines with CO₂ in the Calvin cycle. Ribose and deoxyribose are the sugars of nucleic acids; erythrose is a tetrose.

q: When glucose forms a ring (pyranose) structure, the ring is made of:
o: Five carbon atoms and one oxygen atom
Four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom
x: In the glucose ring, carbon 1 bonds to the oxygen on carbon 5, giving a six-membered ring of five carbons and one oxygen; carbon 6 lies outside the ring. Fructose usually forms a five-membered ring of four carbons and one oxygen.

q: α-glucose and β-glucose differ in:
o: The position of the –OH group on carbon 1 relative to the ring
Having an aldehyde or a ketone group
The position of the –OH group on carbon 6
x: In α-glucose the –OH on carbon 1 lies below the plane of the ring; in β-glucose it lies above. This small difference decides whether starch or cellulose is formed.

q: Glucose, fructose and galactose all have the formula C6H12O6 but different structures. They are therefore:
x: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms are isomers. Isotopes are forms of one element with different numbers of neutrons.

q: Oligosaccharides are carbohydrates that on hydrolysis yield:
o: Hundreds to thousands of monosaccharide units
x: Oligosaccharides have a few (2–10) sugar units; disaccharides such as sucrose are the most common. Polysaccharides have very many units.

q: Cane sugar (sucrose) is made of:
x: Sucrose is a disaccharide of one glucose and one fructose. Lactose is glucose plus galactose, and maltose is two glucose units.

q: Lactose, the sugar of milk, gives on hydrolysis:
x: Lactose is a disaccharide of glucose and galactose. Glucose plus fructose is sucrose; two glucose units make maltose.

q: Maltose, formed during the digestion of starch, consists of:
o: Two α-glucose units joined by an α(1→4) glycosidic bond
Glucose and fructose joined by an α(1→2) bond
Two β-glucose units joined by a β(1→4) bond
Glucose and galactose joined by a β(1→4) bond
x: Amylase breaks starch into maltose, made of two α-glucose units linked between carbon 1 and carbon 4. β(1→4)-linked β-glucose units form cellobiose and cellulose.

q: Two glucose molecules (C6H12O6) combine to form one maltose molecule. The formula of maltose is:
x: Condensation joins the two glucose molecules and removes one water molecule: 2 × C6H12O6 − H2O = C12H22O11.

q: A glycosidic bond links two monosaccharides through:
o: An oxygen atom, formed when water is removed from two –OH groups
A nitrogen atom, formed when ammonia is removed
x: Condensation between two –OH groups removes water and leaves a C–O–C bridge, the glycosidic bond.

q: In which form is carbohydrate mainly transported in the phloem of plants?
x: Sucrose is the main transport sugar of plants. It is soluble, and being non-reducing, it is relatively unreactive on its way through the phloem.

q: Benedict's test gives an orange to brick-red precipitate with reducing sugars. Which of these sugars gives a negative result?
x: Glucose, maltose and lactose are reducing sugars. Sucrose is non-reducing, so Benedict's solution stays blue unless the sucrose is first hydrolysed.

q: Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar because:
o: The reducing groups of both glucose and fructose are used up in forming the glycosidic bond
x: In sucrose, carbon 1 of glucose bonds to carbon 2 of fructose, so neither free aldehyde nor ketone group is left to reduce Benedict's reagent. In maltose one reducing end remains free.

q: A solution turns blue-black when iodine solution is added. It contains:
x: Iodine gives a blue-black colour with starch (mainly its amylose part). Glucose, sucrose and cellulose do not give this colour.

q: Starch consists of two components:
o: Amylose, which is unbranched, and amylopectin, which is branched
x: Amylose is a long unbranched chain of α-glucose; amylopectin is branched. Glycogen is the animal storage polysaccharide, not a part of starch.

q: The branch points in amylopectin and glycogen are formed by which glycosidic linkages?
x: The main chains are α(1→4) linked, and branches start where carbon 1 of one glucose bonds to carbon 6 of another, an α(1→6) link. β(1→4) links are found in cellulose.

q: Compared with amylopectin, glycogen is:
o: More highly branched, with shorter chains between branches
x: Glycogen has branches more often than amylopectin, making it compact and easy to break down quickly. Both are made of α-glucose; glycogen is found in animals and fungi.

q: Glycogen is often called:
x: Glycogen is the storage polysaccharide of animals, so it is called animal starch. Milk sugar is lactose, fruit sugar is fructose and malt sugar is maltose.

q: Cellulose differs from starch in that cellulose is made of:
o: α-glucose units joined by α(1→4) glycosidic bonds
β-glucose units joined by β(1→4) glycosidic bonds
x: Both are glucose polymers, but cellulose uses β-glucose with β(1→4) links, while starch uses α-glucose with α(1→4) (and α(1→6)) links.

q: Humans cannot digest cellulose because they lack an enzyme that can hydrolyse:
x: Human amylase breaks the α(1→4) bonds of starch but not the β(1→4) bonds of cellulose. Humans do not make cellulase, so cellulose passes through as fibre.

q: Cows and goats obtain energy from the cellulose in grass because:
o: Their saliva contains large amounts of amylase
Chewing alone converts cellulose to glucose
Microorganisms in their gut produce cellulase that breaks it down
Their stomach acid hydrolyses cellulose completely
x: Ruminants house bacteria and protozoa that make cellulase and break cellulose down. The animals then absorb the products. Amylase cannot attack cellulose's β links.

q: The most abundant carbohydrate in nature is:
x: Every plant cell wall contains cellulose, making it the most abundant carbohydrate on Earth. Cotton fibres are almost pure cellulose.

q: Chitin, found in arthropod exoskeletons and fungal cell walls, is a polymer of:
x: Chitin is built from N-acetylglucosamine, an amino sugar derived from glucose, so it contains nitrogen. Cellulose, not chitin, is the polymer of plain β-glucose.

q: Cellulose forms strong fibres in plant cell walls mainly because:
o: Its chains are highly branched like glycogen
Its long unbranched chains lie side by side, held together by many hydrogen bonds into microfibrils
Its chains coil into a helix like amylose
x: β(1→4) linkages give straight, unbranched chains. Neighbouring chains form many hydrogen bonds, bundling into microfibrils with great tensile strength.

q: About how many different kinds of amino acids are commonly found in the proteins of living organisms?
x: Proteins of living things are built from about 20 different amino acids. 64 is the number of codons and 4 the number of bases in DNA or RNA.

q: The bond that joins two amino acids together in a protein is called a:
x: Amino acids are linked by peptide bonds. Glycosidic bonds join monosaccharides, ester bonds join fatty acids to glycerol, and phosphodiester bonds join nucleotides.

q: A peptide bond is formed between:
o: The carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, with loss of water
The R groups of two neighbouring amino acids, with loss of water
The amino groups of two amino acids, with addition of water
The carboxyl groups of two amino acids, with addition of water
x: In a condensation reaction the –COOH of one amino acid reacts with the –NH2 of the next; a molecule of water is removed and a –CO–NH– link forms.

q: The 20 amino acids found in proteins differ from one another only in their:
x: Every amino acid has the same backbone: an alpha carbon carrying an amino group, a carboxyl group and a hydrogen. Only the R group varies, giving each amino acid its own properties.

q: Which is the simplest amino acid, in which the R group is just a hydrogen atom?
x: In glycine the R group is a single hydrogen atom. In alanine the R group is a methyl (–CH3) group, which is the next simplest.

q: Amino acids are described as amphoteric because they:
o: Contain both an acidic carboxyl group and a basic amino group
Are soluble in both water and ether
Can join to form both proteins and lipids
x: An amino acid carries a –COOH group that can release H+ and an –NH2 group that can accept H+, so it can act as both an acid and a base.

q: Which amino acid is acidic because its R group carries an extra carboxyl group?
x: Aspartic acid (like glutamic acid) has a second –COOH in its side chain, making it acidic. Lysine has an extra amino group and is basic; glycine and alanine are neutral.

q: A single polypeptide chain is made from 150 amino acids. How many water molecules are released in forming it?
x: Each peptide bond releases one water molecule, and a chain of n amino acids has n – 1 peptide bonds. So 150 amino acids give 149 peptide bonds and 149 water molecules.

q: The first protein whose complete amino acid sequence was worked out, by Frederick Sanger, was:
x: Sanger determined the sequence of the hormone insulin, showing for the first time that a protein has a definite primary structure.

q: Which description of the insulin molecule is correct?
o: A single chain of 51 amino acids held only by hydrogen bonds
Four chains, two alpha and two beta, around haem groups
Two polypeptide chains of 21 and 30 amino acids joined by disulphide bridges
Two chains of 51 amino acids each joined by ionic bonds
x: Insulin has 51 amino acids in two chains, an A chain of 21 and a B chain of 30, linked by disulphide bridges. Four chains with haem groups describes haemoglobin.

q: The alpha helix, a secondary structure of proteins, is held in shape mainly by:
o: Hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups of the backbone
x: In the alpha helix the C=O of one peptide bond forms a hydrogen bond with the N–H of a peptide bond a few residues further along, holding the coil in place.

q: The alpha helix and beta pleated sheet models of protein secondary structure were proposed by:
x: Linus Pauling and Robert Corey described the alpha helix and beta pleated sheet in 1951. Watson and Crick proposed the DNA double helix; Sanger sequenced insulin.

q: The beta pleated sheet is the main secondary structure of which protein?
x: Silk fibroin consists largely of beta pleated sheets of chains lying side by side, joined by hydrogen bonds. Myoglobin and haemoglobin are mostly alpha helix folded into globular shapes.

q: Which bond that stabilises the tertiary structure of a protein is a strong covalent bond?
x: A disulphide bridge (–S–S–) is a covalent bond between the sulphur atoms of two cysteine residues. Hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and hydrophobic interactions are weaker non-covalent forces.

q: A disulphide bridge in a protein is formed between the side chains of two:
x: Cysteine has a sulphur-containing –SH group in its R group; two such groups can be oxidised to form an –S–S– bridge. The other amino acids listed have no sulphur.

q: Haemoglobin is said to have a quaternary structure because it:
o: Is made of four polypeptide chains fitted together
Has its chain coiled into an alpha helix
Contains four different kinds of amino acids
Has four disulphide bridges in a single chain
x: Quaternary structure is the arrangement of two or more polypeptide chains in one functional protein. Haemoglobin has four chains, two alpha and two beta.

q: Which of the following is a fibrous protein?
x: Keratin of hair, nails and horns is a fibrous structural protein. Haemoglobin, insulin and the enzyme pepsin are globular proteins.

q: Which statement correctly describes globular proteins?
o: They are usually soluble in water and have metabolic roles such as enzymes and hormones
They are long insoluble fibres with mainly structural roles
They consist of parallel chains with no folding
They are not affected by heat or changes in pH
x: Globular proteins are folded into compact, roughly spherical shapes and are generally water-soluble; enzymes, antibodies and many hormones are globular. Long insoluble structural fibres describe fibrous proteins.

q: Collagen, found in tendons, skin and bone, is:
o: A globular protein with a single polypeptide chain
A globular protein carrying four haem groups
A fibrous protein made only of beta pleated sheets
A fibrous protein made of three polypeptide chains wound around each other
x: Collagen is the main fibrous protein of connective tissue. Its molecule is a triple helix of three polypeptide chains, which gives great tensile strength.

q: Which protein has a tertiary structure but NO quaternary structure?
x: Myoglobin is a single folded polypeptide chain, so its highest level is tertiary. Haemoglobin has four chains, collagen three and an antibody four, so each has quaternary structure.

q: When a protein is denatured by moderate heat, which level of its structure normally remains intact?
x: Denaturation breaks the weak bonds that hold the folded shape, so secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures are lost. The peptide bonds are not broken, so the amino acid sequence (primary structure) stays the same.

q: Which of the following does NOT normally denature a protein?
o: Storage at a low temperature, such as in a refrigerator
Adding heavy metal ions such as mercury
x: High temperature, extreme pH and heavy metal ions disrupt the bonds that hold a protein's shape. Low temperature only slows molecular movement; activity usually returns on warming.

q: Clear egg white turns solid and white when an egg is boiled. This is because:
o: The peptide bonds of albumin are hydrolysed
New peptide bonds form between albumin molecules
The albumin is converted into fat
x: Heat breaks the hydrogen and other weak bonds of the albumin, which unfolds and coagulates. Peptide bonds remain intact, so this is denaturation, not hydrolysis.

q: Some denatured proteins refold and regain their activity when normal conditions are restored. This shows that:
o: Denaturation breaks all the peptide bonds in a protein
The three-dimensional shape of a protein is determined by its amino acid sequence
Proteins can change their amino acid sequence after folding
The secondary structure is independent of the primary structure
x: Because the sequence (primary structure) is unchanged during denaturation, the chain can fold back into the same shape. This shows that the sequence decides how the chain folds.

q: Complete hydrolysis of a polypeptide produces:
x: Hydrolysis adds water across each peptide bond, breaking the chain into its amino acids. Fatty acids and glycerol come from fats, monosaccharides from carbohydrates.

q: The peptide linkage between two amino acids is represented as:
x: A peptide bond links the carbon of a carbonyl group to the nitrogen of an amino group: –CO–NH–. –CO–O– is an ester link, –O– a glycosidic link and the phosphate link joins nucleotides.

q: In a globular protein dissolved in water, amino acids with non-polar (hydrophobic) R groups are usually found:
o: On the outer surface facing the water
Only at the two ends of the chain
In the interior of the folded molecule
Bonded to water molecules by hydrogen bonds
x: During folding, non-polar side chains cluster together in the centre away from water (hydrophobic interactions), while polar and charged side chains lie on the surface. This helps make globular proteins soluble.

q: Ionic bonds in the tertiary structure of a protein form between:
o: Oppositely charged R groups, such as –NH3+ and –COO–
The C=O and N–H groups of the backbone
x: An ionic bond is an attraction between a positively charged side chain (e.g. of lysine) and a negatively charged one (e.g. of aspartic acid). Cysteine pairs form disulphide bridges, and backbone C=O and N–H form hydrogen bonds.

q: In sickle-cell haemoglobin, one amino acid in each beta chain is replaced by another, and the whole molecule changes shape. The original change is in the protein's:
x: Replacing glutamic acid by valine alters the amino acid sequence, i.e. the primary structure. The altered sequence then changes how the molecules fold and pack, showing that higher levels depend on the primary structure.

q: Which protein is correctly paired with its function?
x: Haemoglobin in red blood cells carries oxygen. Keratin is a structural protein of hair and nails, insulin is a hormone controlling blood glucose, and collagen gives strength to connective tissue.

q: Besides carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, every protein contains:
x: Every amino acid has an amino group, so all proteins contain nitrogen. Many also contain sulphur; iron is found only in certain proteins such as haemoglobin.

q: The general formula of an amino acid is:
x: An amino acid has an alpha carbon bonded to an R group, a hydrogen, an amino group and a carboxyl group: R–CH(NH2)–COOH. R–COOH alone is a fatty acid and R–CO–O–R is an ester.

q: Lipids are insoluble in water but dissolve readily in:
o: Organic solvents such as ether and chloroform
x: Lipids are non-polar, so they do not mix with water but dissolve in non-polar organic solvents such as ether, chloroform, benzene and alcohol.

q: A triglyceride molecule is formed from:
o: Three glycerols and one fatty acid
One glycerol and one fatty acid
Three amino acids and one fatty acid
One glycerol and three fatty acids
x: Each of the three –OH groups of glycerol forms an ester bond with one fatty acid, giving a triglyceride (triacylglycerol).

q: Fatty acids are joined to glycerol in a triglyceride by:
x: The –COOH of each fatty acid condenses with an –OH of glycerol to form an ester bond. Glycosidic bonds link sugars and peptide bonds link amino acids.

q: How many molecules of water are released when one molecule of triglyceride is formed?
x: Three ester bonds are formed, one for each fatty acid, and each condensation releases one water molecule, so three water molecules are released.

q: An ester is formed when:
o: Two alcohols combine and water is added
An acid reacts with an amino group and water is removed
An alcohol reacts with an acid and water is removed
A sugar reacts with phosphate and water is added
x: Esterification is a condensation reaction between an alcohol (–OH) and an acid (–COOH), releasing water. An acid reacting with an amino group gives a peptide (amide) link instead.

q: Chemically, glycerol is:
o: An alcohol with three hydroxyl groups
An alcohol with one hydroxyl group
x: Glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) is a trihydric alcohol: a three-carbon chain with an –OH on each carbon, so it can bind up to three fatty acids.

q: A diacylglycerol contains:
o: Two glycerols bonded to one fatty acid
Glycerol bonded to two phosphate groups
Two fatty acids bonded to each other
Glycerol bonded to two fatty acids
x: Acylglycerols are named by the number of fatty acid (acyl) groups on glycerol: one in a monoacylglycerol, two in a diacylglycerol and three in a triacylglycerol.

q: Which of the following is an unsaturated fatty acid?
x: Oleic acid has one C=C double bond in its chain. Palmitic, stearic and butyric acids have only single bonds between carbon atoms, so they are saturated.

q: Most plant oils are liquid at room temperature mainly because their fatty acids:
o: Are joined to glycerol by peptide bonds
Are unsaturated, and the double bonds lower the melting point
Have more oxygen atoms than animal fats
x: C=C double bonds put kinks in fatty acid chains, so the molecules cannot pack closely and the melting point falls. Animal fats rich in saturated fatty acids are therefore solid at room temperature.

q: Which change in its fatty acids would RAISE the melting point of a fat?
o: Shorter chains and more double bonds
More double bonds with the same chain length
Shorter chains with the same number of double bonds
Longer chains and fewer double bonds
x: Melting point rises with chain length and falls with the number of double bonds. Longer, more saturated chains pack closely and need more heat to separate.

q: The functional group present in every fatty acid is the:
x: A fatty acid is a hydrocarbon chain ending in a carboxyl group (R–COOH). The hydroxyl groups belong to glycerol, the alcohol part of a fat.

q: Linoleic acid has two C=C double bonds in its carbon chain. It is therefore described as:
x: A fatty acid with one double bond is monounsaturated; with two or more it is polyunsaturated. A saturated or fully hydrogenated fatty acid has no C=C double bonds.

q: To make vegetable ghee, hydrogen is added to plant oil in the presence of a catalyst. This turns the oil solid because:
o: New ester bonds are formed with glycerol
The fatty acids are broken into glycerol
Phosphate groups are added to the fatty acids
The double bonds become single bonds, so the fatty acids become more saturated
x: Hydrogenation adds hydrogen across C=C double bonds, making the fatty acid chains saturated and straighter. They pack more closely, so the melting point rises and the fat is solid.

q: A phospholipid differs from a triglyceride in that:
o: All three fatty acids are replaced by phosphate groups
Its fatty acids are joined by peptide bonds
One fatty acid is replaced by a phosphate-containing group
x: A phospholipid has glycerol with two fatty acids; the third –OH carries a phosphate group, often linked to another group such as choline. A triglyceride has three fatty acids.

q: In a phospholipid molecule, the hydrophilic (water-attracting) part is the:
o: Hydrocarbon chain of the longest fatty acid
x: The charged phosphate head is polar and attracts water, while the two non-polar fatty acid tails repel water. This makes phospholipids amphipathic.

q: When phospholipids are placed in water, they arrange themselves as a bilayer in which:
o: The heads face inward and the tails face the water
The tails face inward and the heads face the water on both sides
All molecules lie flat with tails in the water
x: The hydrophobic tails avoid water by pointing towards each other inside the bilayer, while the hydrophilic heads face the water on each side. This is the basis of cell membranes.

q: The main role of phospholipids in cells is to:
o: Form the basic structure of cell membranes
x: Phospholipid bilayers form the framework of the plasma membrane and of the membranes around organelles.

q: Lecithin is a phospholipid in which the phosphate group is linked to:
x: Lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) is made of glycerol, two fatty acids, phosphoric acid and the nitrogen-containing base choline. It is a common membrane phospholipid.

q: A wax is an ester formed between:
o: A long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol other than glycerol
Glycerol, two fatty acids and phosphate
A fatty acid and an amino acid
x: Waxes are esters of a long-chain fatty acid with a long-chain monohydric alcohol, not glycerol. Glycerol with three fatty acids is a triglyceride, and with phosphate it is a phospholipid.

q: The waxy cuticle on the leaves of many plants mainly serves to:
o: Reduce water loss from the leaf surface
x: Waxes are very water-repellent, so a wax layer on leaves, fruits and insect bodies forms a waterproof barrier that cuts down evaporation.

q: Compared with one gram of carbohydrate, one gram of fat on complete oxidation releases about:
x: Fats yield roughly twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates or proteins, which is why they are a compact energy store.

q: Which of the following is NOT a function of lipids?
o: Acting as the main catalysts of metabolic reactions
Forming the bilayer of cell membranes
x: Lipids store energy, insulate the body and build membranes. Metabolic reactions are catalysed by enzymes, which are proteins, not lipids.

q: Saturated fatty acids have the general formula CnH2n+1COOH. How many C=C double bonds are present in a fatty acid with the formula C17H29COOH?
x: A saturated fatty acid with 17 carbons in its chain would be C17H35COOH. This one has 6 fewer hydrogen atoms, and each C=C double bond removes 2 hydrogens, so it has 3 double bonds (it is linolenic acid).

q: Triglycerides are often called neutral fats because they:
o: Contain equal numbers of acids and bases
Carry no charged groups and are non-polar
Have a pH of exactly 7 when dissolved in water
x: In a triglyceride the –COOH of each fatty acid has been used up in an ester bond, so no acidic or charged groups remain; the molecule is non-polar and uncharged.

q: When a fat is boiled with sodium hydroxide, the products are glycerol and:
x: Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) breaks the ester bonds; the fatty acids form sodium salts, which are soap, and glycerol is released.

q: Most naturally occurring fatty acids have:
o: An odd number of carbon atoms
A ring of six carbon atoms
An amino group on the second carbon
An even number of carbon atoms
x: Natural fatty acids usually have an even number of carbon atoms, commonly 14 to 22, because they are built up two carbons at a time.

q: Which formula represents an unsaturated fatty acid?
x: A saturated fatty acid fits the formula CnH2n+1COOH. C17H35COOH (stearic), C15H31COOH (palmitic) and C3H7COOH (butyric) fit it; C17H33COOH (oleic acid) has two fewer hydrogens, showing one C=C double bond.

q: The thick layer of fat (blubber) under the skin of whales and seals mainly provides:
x: Fat conducts heat poorly, so a thick subcutaneous fat layer insulates animals in cold water; it also serves as an energy reserve.

q: Unlike proteins and polysaccharides, triglycerides are not considered polymers because:
o: They are not built from many repeating monomer units
They are formed without condensation reactions
They contain only one kind of bond
x: A polymer is a long chain of many similar monomers. A triglyceride is a single glycerol joined to just three fatty acids, so it is a relatively small molecule, not a polymer, even though it forms by condensation.

q: In plants, triglycerides (oils) are stored mainly in:
o: Seeds, such as those of sunflower and mustard
x: Many seeds store oil as an energy reserve for the germinating seedling; this is why oils are extracted from seeds of sunflower, mustard, cotton and groundnut.

q: On complete hydrolysis, a lipid gives glycerol, two fatty acids, phosphoric acid and choline. The lipid is:
x: Glycerol plus two fatty acids plus phosphate and choline is the make-up of a phospholipid (lecithin). A triglyceride or diacylglycerol contains no phosphate, and a wax has no glycerol.

q: The ester linkage found in fats can be represented as:
x: An ester bond joins the carbonyl carbon of the acid to the oxygen of the alcohol: –CO–O–. –CO–NH– is a peptide bond and –S–S– a disulphide bridge.

q: The sugar present in RNA nucleotides is:
x: RNA (ribonucleic acid) contains the five-carbon sugar ribose. DNA contains deoxyribose.

q: Which nitrogenous base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
x: RNA contains uracil in place of thymine. Adenine and cytosine are present in both DNA and RNA.

q: An RNA nucleotide is made up of:
o: Deoxyribose, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base
Ribose, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base
Ribose, a fatty acid and a nitrogenous base
Ribose, a phosphate group and an amino acid
x: Each ribonucleotide consists of a ribose sugar, a phosphate group and one of the bases adenine, guanine, cytosine or uracil.

q: Where an RNA molecule folds back and pairs with itself, as in the arms of tRNA, uracil pairs with:
x: In RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine and pairs with adenine by hydrogen bonds; guanine pairs with cytosine.

q: Nucleotides in an RNA strand are joined together by:
o: Phosphodiester bonds between the sugar of one and the phosphate of the next
x: The phosphate of one nucleotide links the 3' carbon of one ribose to the 5' carbon of the next, forming a sugar–phosphate backbone held by phosphodiester bonds.

q: Which statement correctly states a difference between RNA and DNA?
o: RNA is usually single-stranded, while DNA is double-stranded
RNA contains thymine, while DNA contains uracil
RNA contains deoxyribose, while DNA contains ribose
RNA is found only in the nucleus, while DNA is found only in the cytoplasm
x: RNA is usually a single strand, while DNA is a double helix. The other statements reverse the facts: RNA has ribose and uracil, and RNA is found in both nucleus and cytoplasm.

q: The type of RNA that carries the genetic message from DNA to the ribosomes is:
x: mRNA is transcribed from DNA in the nucleus and carries the coded instructions, as codons, to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm.

q: Which type of RNA makes up the largest proportion of the total RNA in a cell?
x: rRNA forms about 80% of the cell's RNA because ribosomes are very numerous. tRNA is about 15% and mRNA only a few per cent.

q: The smallest of the three main types of RNA is:
x: tRNA molecules are short, only about 70 to 90 nucleotides long. mRNA and rRNA molecules are much longer.

q: When drawn flat in two dimensions, a tRNA molecule has the shape of a:
x: Base pairing between parts of the single tRNA strand produces stems and loops, giving a cloverleaf shape in two dimensions.

q: The part of a tRNA molecule that recognises a codon on mRNA is the:
o: Amino acid attachment site at the 3' end
x: The anticodon is a set of three bases in one loop of tRNA that pairs with the complementary codon on mRNA, placing the correct amino acid.

q: An amino acid is attached to its tRNA molecule at:
o: The 3' end, which ends in the bases CCA
The 5' end, which carries a phosphate
The middle of the longest loop
x: Each tRNA ends at its 3' end with the sequence CCA, and the amino acid binds to the terminal adenine nucleotide. The anticodon is at the opposite end of the molecule.

q: A codon on mRNA reads AUG. Read base by base in line with this codon, the anticodon of the tRNA that pairs with it is:
x: Pairing A with U, U with A and G with C, the anticodon is UAC. TAC would be a DNA sequence, since RNA has no thymine.

q: Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) combines with which molecules to form ribosomes?
x: Each ribosome is made of rRNA together with many proteins, arranged in a large and a small subunit.

q: In eukaryotic cells, ribosomal RNA is made mainly in the:
x: The nucleolus contains the genes for rRNA; there rRNA is transcribed and begins assembly with proteins into ribosomal subunits.

q: All three main types of RNA are made by copying a DNA template in a process called:
x: Transcription is the synthesis of RNA on a DNA template by RNA polymerase. Translation is protein synthesis on ribosomes, and replication is the copying of DNA.

q: A codon on mRNA is made up of:
x: The genetic code is a triplet code: each codon is a sequence of three nucleotides that specifies one amino acid or a stop signal.

q: The coding region of an mRNA, not counting the stop codon, codes for a polypeptide of 120 amino acids. How many nucleotides does this region contain?
x: Each amino acid is coded by a codon of three nucleotides, so 120 amino acids need 120 × 3 = 360 nucleotides.

q: The main function of transfer RNA (tRNA) is to:
o: Bring specific amino acids to the ribosome during protein synthesis
Carry the genetic code from the nucleus to the cytoplasm
Form the structural framework of the ribosome
Act as the genetic material of the cell
x: Each tRNA carries one kind of amino acid and delivers it to the ribosome, matching its anticodon to the mRNA codon. Carrying the code is the role of mRNA, and forming the ribosome is the role of rRNA.

q: In which of the following is RNA the hereditary material?
x: Tobacco mosaic virus has an RNA genome. Bacteriophage T4, bacteria such as E. coli and humans all use DNA as their genetic material.

q: Analysis of a sample of mRNA shows that 30% of its bases are adenine. What can be said about its uracil content?
o: It cannot be predicted from the adenine content, because mRNA is single-stranded
x: Equal amounts of paired bases apply only to double-stranded molecules. mRNA is a single strand, so its adenine and uracil contents are independent.

q: The pyrimidine bases found in RNA are:
x: RNA has the purines adenine and guanine and the pyrimidines cytosine and uracil. Thymine occurs in DNA, not RNA.

q: Ribose differs from deoxyribose in that ribose has:
o: A hydroxyl (–OH) group on carbon 2 instead of a hydrogen atom
x: Both are five-carbon sugars. Deoxyribose lacks the oxygen at carbon 2 (it has –H there), while ribose carries an –OH group on carbon 2.

q: In a eukaryotic cell, mRNA moves from the nucleus to the cytoplasm through the:
x: mRNA is made in the nucleus and passes out to the cytoplasm through pores in the nuclear envelope, then binds to ribosomes.

q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of tRNA?
o: It carries the codons for an entire polypeptide
It carries a specific amino acid
It shows a cloverleaf shape when drawn flat
x: tRNA has an anticodon, binds one amino acid and has a cloverleaf shape. The sequence of codons for a whole polypeptide is carried by mRNA.

q: A cell needs at least 20 different kinds of tRNA because:
o: Each tRNA can be used only once
Each ribosome needs its own tRNA
Each kind of tRNA carries only one specific kind of amino acid
tRNA forms the 20 proteins of the ribosome
x: Each tRNA is specific for one amino acid, so at least one kind of tRNA is needed for each of the 20 amino acids used in proteins.

q: Which sequence of events in a eukaryotic cell is in the correct order?
o: tRNA anticodons pair with DNA, mRNA leaves the nucleus, and then mRNA is transcribed on a ribosome
mRNA is transcribed in the nucleus, leaves through nuclear pores, binds a ribosome, and tRNA anticodons pair with its codons
mRNA binds a ribosome in the nucleus, is then transcribed, and tRNA carries it out through the pores
rRNA copies the DNA, leaves the nucleus as mRNA, and tRNA joins the codons together
x: mRNA is first made on the DNA template in the nucleus, then exits to the cytoplasm, attaches to a ribosome, and tRNAs bring amino acids by matching their anticodons to its codons.

q: The codon on mRNA that signals the start of translation is:
x: AUG is the start codon and also codes for methionine. UAA, UGA and UAG are stop codons that end translation.

q: A group of several ribosomes attached to the same mRNA molecule, all making the same polypeptide, is called a:
x: Several ribosomes can translate one mRNA at the same time; together they form a polysome (polyribosome). A nucleosome is a DNA–histone unit and a lysosome is a digestive vesicle.

q: Complete hydrolysis of a tRNA molecule would yield:
o: Deoxyribose, phosphoric acid and the bases adenine, guanine, cytosine and thymine
Ribose, phosphoric acid and the bases adenine, guanine, cytosine and uracil
Ribose, amino acids and the bases adenine and uracil only
Glycerol, fatty acids and phosphoric acid
x: tRNA is a nucleic acid, so it breaks down into its nucleotide parts: ribose, phosphate and the four RNA bases A, G, C and U. Deoxyribose and thymine come from DNA.

q: Which statement about mRNA is correct?
o: It is the most abundant type of RNA in the cell
Its base sequence is complementary to the template strand of DNA
It contains thymine instead of uracil
x: mRNA is built by base pairing with the template strand of DNA, so its sequence is complementary to that strand. Anticodons are on tRNA, rRNA is the most abundant RNA, and RNA uses uracil.

q: A glycolipid is formed by the combination of:
o: A nucleic acid and a protein
x: Glycolipids are lipids with a carbohydrate (sugar) chain attached. Lipid plus protein gives a lipoprotein, and protein plus carbohydrate gives a glycoprotein.

q: A glycoprotein consists of:
o: A lipid with carbohydrate chains attached
A protein with carbohydrate chains attached
A protein with lipid molecules attached
x: Glycoproteins are proteins carrying covalently attached carbohydrate (oligosaccharide) chains. A lipid with sugar chains is a glycolipid.

q: The term 'conjugated molecule' refers to a molecule that is:
o: Formed by the union of two different classes of biomolecules
Made of a single repeating monomer only
Formed when two identical monosaccharides join
Built only from amino acids joined by peptide bonds
x: Conjugated molecules form when molecules of two different categories combine, for example lipid with carbohydrate (glycolipid) or protein with nucleic acid (nucleoprotein).

q: Which of the following is NOT a conjugated molecule?
x: Starch is a simple polysaccharide made only of glucose units. Chromatin is a nucleoprotein, mucin is a glycoprotein and a lipoprotein combines lipid with protein.

q: Lipoproteins in blood plasma are important mainly because they:
o: Transport water-insoluble lipids such as cholesterol and triglycerides
Carry oxygen from the lungs to the tissues
Store genetic information for protein synthesis
Act as the main buffer of blood pH
x: Lipids do not dissolve in watery plasma, so they are carried packed with proteins as lipoproteins. Oxygen is carried by haemoglobin, not lipoproteins.

q: Chromatin in the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell is chemically a:
o: Glycoprotein made of protein and sugar
Lipoprotein made of lipid and protein
Glycolipid made of lipid and sugar
Nucleoprotein made of DNA and proteins
x: Chromatin consists of DNA combined with proteins, mainly histones, so it is a nucleoprotein.

q: Which pair of cell structures are both nucleoproteins?
x: Ribosomes are made of rRNA and protein, and chromosomes of DNA and histone proteins; both combine nucleic acid with protein. Lysosomes, centrioles and the cell wall are not nucleoproteins.

q: In the plasma membrane, the carbohydrate chains of glycolipids and glycoproteins are found:
o: On the inner surface, facing the cytoplasm
Buried in the hydrophobic core of the bilayer
On the outer surface, facing the outside of the cell
Only in the membranes of the nucleus
x: The sugar chains of membrane glycolipids and glycoproteins project from the outer (extracellular) surface of the plasma membrane, where they can interact with other cells and molecules.

q: The carbohydrate-rich coat on the outer surface of many animal cells, called the glycocalyx, is formed mainly by:
o: Cellulose fibres secreted by the cell
Sugar chains of glycoproteins and glycolipids
x: The glycocalyx is made of the carbohydrate parts of membrane glycoproteins and glycolipids. Cellulose is a plant cell wall material, not part of an animal cell coat.

q: An important role of membrane glycoproteins and glycolipids is:
o: Storage of energy for the cell
x: Their surface sugar chains act as recognition markers, allowing cells to identify one another and stick together, for example in tissue formation and immune responses.

q: Mucus secreted by goblet cells is slimy and protective mainly because it contains:
x: Mucins are heavily glycosylated proteins (glycoproteins) that bind water and form slimy mucus. Chylomicrons are blood lipoproteins and histones are DNA-binding proteins.

q: Antibodies (immunoglobulins) produced by plasma cells are chemically:
x: Antibodies are proteins with carbohydrate chains attached, so they are glycoproteins. They are not combined with lipids or nucleic acids.

q: Which of the following hormones is a glycoprotein?
x: FSH is a protein hormone with attached carbohydrate, a glycoprotein. Testosterone is a steroid, while adrenaline and thyroxine are small amino-acid-derived hormones.

q: Cerebrosides, which are abundant in the brain and in the myelin sheath of nerve fibres, belong to the group:
x: Cerebrosides are lipids carrying a sugar unit, so they are glycolipids. Glycolipids are especially plentiful in the membranes of nerve tissue.

q: In a eukaryotic cell, the carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins are added and modified mainly in the:
x: Proteins made on rough ER receive sugar chains there, and the Golgi apparatus further modifies them before packaging. Mitochondria, nucleolus and centrioles do not glycosylate proteins.

q: Which pairing of a conjugated molecule with its components is correct?
x: A nucleoprotein combines nucleic acid with protein. A glycoprotein is protein plus carbohydrate, a lipoprotein is lipid plus protein, and a glycolipid is lipid plus carbohydrate.

q: In a conjugated protein such as a lipoprotein, the non-protein part attached to the protein is called the:
x: The non-protein component of a conjugated protein is its prosthetic group; in a lipoprotein this is the lipid. The apoprotein is the protein part itself.

q: Histone proteins bind tightly to DNA in nucleoproteins because histones are:
o: Rich in acidic, negatively charged amino acids
Made mostly of hydrophobic amino acids
Linked to DNA by peptide bonds
Rich in basic, positively charged amino acids
x: Histones contain many lysine and arginine residues, which are positively charged and attract the negatively charged phosphate groups of DNA. Acidic proteins would repel DNA.

q: A nucleosome, the basic unit of chromatin, consists of DNA wound around a core of:
x: In a nucleosome the DNA wraps around an octamer of histones, two each of four histone types. Linker DNA joins one nucleosome to the next.

q: The main role of histone proteins in the nucleoprotein chromatin is to:
o: Package and coil long DNA molecules into compact chromosomes
Act as the genetic material passed to offspring
Carry amino acids to the ribosomes
Join nucleotides together during DNA synthesis
x: Histones organise DNA into nucleosomes and higher coils, packing very long DNA into the small nucleus. DNA, not histone, is the genetic material.

q: A virus such as tobacco mosaic virus, made of an RNA core surrounded by a protein coat, is chemically a:
x: A simple virus particle combines a nucleic acid (here RNA) with protein, which fits the definition of a nucleoprotein.

q: Of the plasma lipoproteins, the one with the highest proportion of lipid and therefore the lowest density is:
x: Lipid is less dense than protein, so the more lipid a lipoprotein carries, the lower its density. Chylomicrons, carrying dietary fat from the intestine, are mostly triglyceride and the least dense.

q: The density of a lipoprotein increases as:
o: The proportion of lipid in it increases
The amount of cholesterol in it increases
The proportion of protein in it increases
x: Protein is denser than lipid, so lipoproteins richer in protein are denser. HDL has the most protein and the highest density; larger, lipid-rich particles are less dense.

q: High-density lipoprotein (HDL) is often called 'good cholesterol' because it:
o: Carries cholesterol from body tissues back to the liver
Carries cholesterol from the liver to body tissues
Carries dietary fat from the intestine into the blood
Deposits cholesterol in the walls of arteries
x: HDL collects excess cholesterol from tissues and returns it to the liver. LDL carries cholesterol out to the tissues, and chylomicrons carry dietary fat from the intestine.

q: A blood test shows a person has a high level of low-density lipoprotein (LDL). This is associated with:
o: Greater removal of cholesterol by the liver
Lower risk of narrowing of the arteries
Greater transport of oxygen to the tissues
Greater risk of cholesterol deposits in artery walls
x: LDL delivers cholesterol to tissues, and high LDL is linked with cholesterol deposits in arteries (atherosclerosis). Removing cholesterol to the liver is the job of HDL.

q: Which statement about lipoproteins is correct?
o: They store the genetic information of the cell
They allow water-insoluble lipids to be carried in blood plasma
They are made of lipid and carbohydrate only
They are found only inside the nucleus
x: Lipoproteins wrap lipids with protein so they can travel in watery plasma. Genetic information is in nucleic acids, and lipid plus carbohydrate would be a glycolipid.

q: Insulin receptors and many other hormone receptors on the cell surface are chemically:
x: Cell-surface hormone receptors such as the insulin receptor are membrane proteins with carbohydrate chains, that is, glycoproteins. Phospholipids form the bilayer but do not act as specific receptors here.

q: The ABO blood group antigens on the surface of red blood cells owe their specificity to:
o: The fatty-acid tails of membrane phospholipids
The haemoglobin inside the red blood cell
Carbohydrate chains on membrane glycolipids and glycoproteins
x: The antigens of the different blood groups differ only in the sugars at the ends of carbohydrate chains attached to membrane lipids and proteins. This is an example of sugar chains acting as recognition markers.

q: Glycoproteins are well suited to act as 'identity markers' on the cell surface because their:
o: Sugar chains are identical in all cells of all organisms
Branched sugar chains vary in sequence and project outside the cell
Protein part stores energy for recognition
Carbohydrate part lies hidden inside the bilayer
x: Sugar chains can be branched and assembled in many different sequences, giving each cell type a distinctive surface pattern exposed to the outside. Identical or hidden chains could not serve as markers.

q: Complete hydrolysis of a glycoprotein would yield:
x: A glycoprotein is protein plus carbohydrate, so hydrolysis gives amino acids from the protein and monosaccharides from the sugar chains. Nucleotides with amino acids would come from a nucleoprotein.

q: In the plasma membrane, glycolipids are located:
o: In the inner layer of the bilayer only
In the outer layer of the bilayer only
Equally in both layers of the bilayer
Only in the membrane of the nucleus
x: Glycolipids sit in the outer (extracellular) leaflet with their sugar chains facing outwards. This asymmetric placement lets them take part in recognition at the cell surface.

q: The double helical model of DNA was proposed in 1953 by:
x: James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double helix in 1953. Beadle and Tatum gave the one gene–one enzyme idea, and Hershey–Chase and Meselson–Stahl did later experiments on DNA.

q: Watson and Crick built their model of DNA largely using X-ray diffraction pictures obtained by:
x: The X-ray diffraction data of Franklin and Wilkins showed DNA was a helix with regular repeats. Chargaff supplied base-ratio data, not X-ray images.

q: A single DNA nucleotide is made of:
o: Ribose, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base
Deoxyribose, an amino acid and a phosphate group
Deoxyribose, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base
Glucose, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base
x: Each DNA nucleotide has a pentose sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group and one of four nitrogenous bases. Ribose is the sugar of RNA.

q: Deoxyribose in DNA differs from ribose in RNA in that deoxyribose:
o: Lacks an oxygen atom at carbon 2
Lacks an oxygen atom at carbon 5
Has six carbon atoms instead of five
Has an extra phosphate at carbon 3
x: 'Deoxy' means one oxygen less: at carbon 2 deoxyribose has H where ribose has an OH group. Both are five-carbon sugars.

q: Adenine and guanine are classed as purines because they have:
o: Two fused rings of carbon and nitrogen atoms
A phosphate group in their ring
A sugar ring instead of a base ring
x: Purines (adenine, guanine) are double-ring bases. Pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) have a single ring.

q: Which nitrogenous base is found in DNA but not in RNA?
x: Thymine occurs in DNA and is replaced by uracil in RNA. Cytosine, guanine and adenine occur in both.

q: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine by:
x: Adenine and thymine form two hydrogen bonds, while guanine and cytosine form three. Phosphodiester bonds join nucleotides along one strand, not across the strands.

q: Two DNA molecules have the same length. Molecule X has a higher proportion of guanine–cytosine pairs than molecule Y. Compared with Y, molecule X will:
o: Need less heat to separate its two strands
Need more heat to separate its two strands
Have fewer base pairs per turn
x: Each G–C pair has three hydrogen bonds against two for A–T, so a G–C-rich molecule is held together more strongly and needs more heat to separate. Diameter and pairs per turn stay the same.

q: In a double-stranded DNA molecule, 20% of the bases are adenine. What percentage are cytosine?
x: Adenine equals thymine, so A + T = 40%. The remaining 60% is shared equally between guanine and cytosine, giving 30% cytosine.

q: A double-stranded DNA sample contains 35% guanine. The percentage of thymine in it is:
x: Guanine equals cytosine, so G + C = 70%. The other 30% is adenine plus thymine in equal amounts, so thymine is 15%.

q: A double-stranded DNA molecule has 2000 nucleotides, of which 600 contain thymine. How many contain guanine?
x: Thymine = adenine = 600, so A + T = 1200. The remaining 800 are guanine and cytosine in equal numbers, giving 400 guanine.

q: A DNA segment has 50 base pairs, of which 20 are adenine–thymine pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold its two strands together?
x: 20 A–T pairs give 20 × 2 = 40 hydrogen bonds; the other 30 pairs are G–C with 30 × 3 = 90. The total is 130.

q: According to Chargaff's rules, which ratio always equals 1 in double-stranded DNA?
x: Because every purine pairs with a pyrimidine, total purines (adenine + guanine) equal total pyrimidines (thymine + cytosine). The other ratios differ between species.

q: Which base ratio of double-stranded DNA differs from one species to another?
x: Adenine/thymine, guanine/cytosine and purines/pyrimidines are always 1 because of base pairing. The proportion of A–T to G–C pairs depends on the species.

q: If one strand of a DNA molecule has 30% adenine and 20% thymine, the complementary strand will have:
x: Each thymine on the first strand pairs with an adenine on the other strand, so the complementary strand has 20% adenine (and 30% thymine).

q: A DNA virus has bases in the ratio adenine 25%, thymine 33%, guanine 24%, cytosine 18%. The most reasonable conclusion is that its DNA is:
o: Made of RNA instead of DNA
x: In double-stranded DNA adenine must equal thymine and guanine must equal cytosine. These unequal values show the bases are not paired, so the DNA is single-stranded.

q: The diameter of the DNA double helix is about:
x: The double helix has a uniform width of about 2 nm (20 Å). 3.4 nm is the length of one complete turn and 0.34 nm the distance between neighbouring base pairs.

q: In the Watson–Crick model, the distance between two successive base pairs along the helix is:
x: Adjacent base pairs are stacked 0.34 nm apart. Ten of them make one complete turn of 3.4 nm.

q: One complete turn of the DNA double helix contains about:
o: 10 base pairs and is 2 nm long
10 base pairs and is 3.4 nm long
20 base pairs and is 3.4 nm long
3 base pairs and is 0.34 nm long
x: A full turn has about 10 base pairs, each 0.34 nm apart, giving a pitch of 3.4 nm. The 2 nm figure is the diameter, not the length of a turn.

q: Using the Watson–Crick dimensions, what is the length of a DNA molecule containing 1000 base pairs?
x: Each base pair adds 0.34 nm, so 1000 × 0.34 nm = 340 nm.

q: A double-stranded DNA molecule makes 150 complete turns. How many nucleotides does it contain in total?
x: Each turn has 10 base pairs, so 150 turns = 1500 base pairs. Each base pair has two nucleotides, giving 3000 nucleotides.
