q: The two strands of DNA are described as antiparallel because:
o: Both strands run 5′ to 3′ in the same direction
The strands do not twist around each other
One strand runs 5′ to 3′ while its partner runs 3′ to 5′
One strand is DNA and the other is RNA
x: The partner strands run in opposite chemical directions: where one has a 5′ end, the other has a 3′ end.

q: In the DNA double helix, the sugar–phosphate backbones lie:
o: On the outside, with the bases stacked inside
On the inside, with the bases facing outward
Along the central axis of the helix
Between each pair of complementary bases
x: The alternating sugar and phosphate groups form the outer backbones, while the paired bases point inwards like the steps of a twisted ladder.

q: Adjacent nucleotides within one strand of DNA are joined by:
x: A phosphate links carbon 3 of one sugar to carbon 5 of the next, forming a phosphodiester bond. Hydrogen bonds hold the two strands together, not neighbours in one strand.

q: The nitrogenous base of a nucleotide is attached to carbon number 1 of deoxyribose by a:
x: The base joins the 1′ carbon of the sugar through a (N-)glycosidic bond. Phosphodiester bonds involve the phosphate, and hydrogen bonds link paired bases.

q: When DNA is heated or unzipped, the two strands separate because of the breaking of:
o: Glycosidic bonds between sugar and base
x: The strands are held together only by weak hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, which break on heating. The strong covalent backbone bonds stay intact.

q: A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine in DNA. The result of this is that the double helix:
o: Can contain uracil in place of thymine
Has bases on the outside of the helix
Has both strands running in the same direction
Has the same width along its whole length
x: A double-ring purine paired with a single-ring pyrimidine always gives a pair of the same size, so the helix stays a uniform 2 nm wide.

q: One strand of DNA has the sequence 5′-ATGCCA-3′. Its complementary strand is:
x: Adenine pairs with thymine and guanine with cytosine, and the partner strand runs in the opposite direction. Uracil is found in RNA, not DNA.

q: In the Watson–Crick model, the two strands of DNA coil around a common axis to form a:
x: Watson and Crick described two strands wound round each other in a right-handed double helix, like a twisted ladder.

q: In a DNA nucleotide, the phosphate group is attached to which carbon of deoxyribose?
x: The phosphate is bonded to the 5′ carbon; the base is attached to the 1′ carbon. In the strand, the 3′ carbon links to the next phosphate.

q: A nucleoside differs from a nucleotide in that a nucleoside:
x: A nucleoside is just a base joined to a pentose sugar. Adding a phosphate group to it makes a nucleotide.

q: Which is NOT a feature of the Watson–Crick model of DNA?
o: The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds
The two strands run in opposite directions
The nitrogenous bases lie on the outside of the helix
Adenine pairs with thymine and guanine with cytosine
x: In the model the bases are inside the helix and the sugar–phosphate backbones are outside. The other three statements are true features of the model.

q: A gene is best defined as:
o: A sequence of nucleotides in DNA that codes for a polypeptide
A sequence of amino acids that codes for a nucleotide
A whole chromosome made of DNA and histones
A single nucleotide pair in DNA
x: A gene is a particular sequence of nucleotides, part of a DNA molecule, that carries the code for making one polypeptide.

q: A codon is:
o: A sequence of three amino acids in a polypeptide
A group of genes on one chromosome
A sequence of three nucleotides on mRNA that specifies an amino acid
x: The genetic code is read in triplets: each codon of three mRNA nucleotides stands for one amino acid or a stop signal.

q: With four different bases read three at a time, the total number of possible codons is:
x: Four bases in each of three positions give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 codons. 16 would be the number for a two-base code.

q: The genetic code cannot be a doublet (two-base) code because:
o: Two bases cannot bind to a ribosome
There would be too many combinations for 20 amino acids
Only 16 combinations are possible, fewer than the 20 amino acids
mRNA has only two kinds of bases
x: Two bases from four give 4 × 4 = 16 combinations, too few for 20 amino acids. A triplet code gives 64, which is more than enough.

q: Which of the following is a stop (termination) codon?
x: UAA, UAG and UGA are the three stop codons, which code for no amino acid. AUG is the start codon (methionine) and UGG codes for tryptophan.

q: The codon AUG serves as the:
o: Stop codon and codes for no amino acid
Start codon and codes for no amino acid
Stop codon and codes for methionine
Start codon and codes for methionine
x: AUG marks where translation begins and also specifies the amino acid methionine.

q: Ignoring the stop codon, the minimum number of nucleotides needed in a gene's coding sequence to specify a polypeptide of 200 amino acids is:
x: Each amino acid needs one codon of three nucleotides, so 200 × 3 = 600 nucleotides.

q: The coding sequence of an mRNA, from the start codon up to and including the stop codon, has 900 nucleotides. How many amino acids will the polypeptide contain?
x: 900 ÷ 3 = 300 codons. The last one is a stop codon, which codes for no amino acid, leaving 299 amino acids.

q: The 'one gene–one enzyme' hypothesis was put forward by Beadle and Tatum from their work on:
x: Beadle and Tatum studied mutant strains of the mould Neurospora that could not make particular enzymes, showing each gene controls one enzyme.

q: The 'one gene–one enzyme' idea was later changed to 'one gene–one polypeptide' because:
o: Many proteins are made of polypeptide chains coded by different genes
Genes were found to code for carbohydrates as well
Enzymes were found to be made of nucleic acids
One gene was found to code for many unrelated enzymes
x: Many proteins, including many enzymes, have more than one kind of polypeptide chain, and each kind is coded by its own gene. So a gene codes for a polypeptide, not always a whole enzyme.

q: Adult haemoglobin contains two kinds of polypeptide chains, alpha and beta. According to the one gene–one polypeptide concept, the minimum number of different genes needed to code for its polypeptides is:
x: Each kind of polypeptide needs its own gene, so two different chains (alpha and beta) need at least two different genes, even though the molecule has four chains in total.

q: The genetic code is described as degenerate because:
o: One codon can code for several amino acids
Most amino acids are coded by more than one codon
Some codons are destroyed during translation
x: With 61 sense codons for 20 amino acids, most amino acids have two or more codons. Each codon still specifies only one amino acid, so the code is not ambiguous.

q: The anticodon that pairs with a codon during protein synthesis is found on:
x: Each tRNA carries an anticodon of three bases that pairs with the matching codon on mRNA, bringing the correct amino acid.

q: A triplet on the template strand of DNA reads TAC. The mRNA codon copied from it is:
x: mRNA is complementary to the template: thymine gives adenine, adenine gives uracil (RNA has no thymine), and cytosine gives guanine. So TAC becomes AUG.

q: An mRNA codon reads GCU. The anticodon on the tRNA that pairs with it is:
x: The anticodon is complementary: guanine pairs with cytosine, cytosine with guanine, and uracil with adenine, giving CGA. Thymine does not occur in tRNA.

q: A gene determines the structure of a polypeptide by specifying its:
x: The order of codons in the gene fixes the order of amino acids in the polypeptide, and this sequence decides how the chain folds and works.

q: In sickle-cell anaemia, a change of a single base in the gene for the beta chain of haemoglobin results in:
o: Loss of the entire beta chain
Addition of an extra haem group
Replacement of all the amino acids of the beta chain
Valine replacing glutamic acid at one position of the beta chain
x: One base substitution alters one codon, so glutamic acid at the sixth position is replaced by valine. This single change is enough to alter the shape of haemoglobin and red cells.

q: The specific position of a gene on a chromosome is called its:
x: A locus is the fixed place a gene occupies on a chromosome. Alleles are alternative forms of a gene found at the same locus.

q: The coded information of a gene is carried from the nucleus to the ribosomes by:
x: The gene's code is transcribed into mRNA, which leaves the nucleus and is read by ribosomes. tRNA brings amino acids, and rRNA is part of the ribosome.

q: Which statement about the genetic code is correct?
o: Each organism has its own completely different code
Each codon codes for several different amino acids
The same codons code for the same amino acids in almost all organisms
Codons are made of four nucleotides each
x: The genetic code is nearly universal: a given codon specifies the same amino acid in bacteria, plants and animals. Codons are triplets, and each specifies one amino acid.

q: The mRNA sequence AUGUUUGGC is read by the ribosome as:
o: Overlapping codons: AUG, UGU, GUU and so on
Two codons of four and five bases
x: The code is read in non-overlapping triplets from the start codon, so these nine bases form three codons.

q: A single extra nucleotide is inserted near the start of a gene's coding sequence. The most likely effect on the polypeptide is that:
o: Almost every amino acid after that point is changed
Only one amino acid is changed
One extra amino acid is added and the rest stay the same
x: Inserting one base shifts the reading frame, so every codon after it is read differently (a frameshift). This usually changes most of the following amino acids or brings in an early stop codon.

q: Three nucleotides forming exactly one complete codon are deleted from the middle of a gene. The polypeptide made will most likely:
o: Have every following amino acid changed
Lack one amino acid but be otherwise unchanged
Be exactly the same as before
x: Removing a whole codon takes out one amino acid but keeps the reading frame intact, so the codons after it are read normally. A one-base deletion, by contrast, would cause a frameshift.

q: Of the 64 codons, how many code for amino acids?
x: Three of the 64 codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) are stop signals, leaving 61 sense codons for the 20 amino acids.

q: The number of different amino acids coded for by the genetic code is:
x: The genetic code specifies 20 standard amino acids. 64 is the total number of codons and 61 the number that code for amino acids.

q: The correct order of the flow of information from a gene is:
x: The gene in DNA is transcribed into mRNA, and the mRNA is translated on ribosomes into a polypeptide.

q: When a ribosome reaches the codon UAA on an mRNA:
o: Translation stops and the polypeptide is released
The amino acid methionine is added
The amino acid tyrosine is added
x: UAA is a stop codon; no tRNA carries an amino acid for it, so the finished polypeptide is released. AUG, not UAA, starts translation with methionine.

q: Which statement about a gene is NOT correct?
o: It is a part of a DNA molecule
It is a sequence of nucleotides
It is made of a chain of amino acids
It codes for the formation of a polypeptide
x: A gene is a stretch of DNA made of nucleotides; it codes for a polypeptide, which is the chain of amino acids. The gene itself is not made of amino acids.

q: A base substitution changes the third base of a codon, yet the polypeptide made is unchanged. This is best explained by the fact that the genetic code is:
o: Degenerate, with several codons for one amino acid
x: Because most amino acids have several codons that often differ only in the third base, a change there may still code for the same amino acid. Universality and non-overlap do not explain this.

q: When a gene is transcribed, the mRNA is copied from:
o: Only one of the two DNA strands, the template strand
Both DNA strands at the same time
The protein coded by the gene
x: Only one strand of the gene, the template strand, is used to make mRNA. The mRNA is complementary to the template strand.

q: Nirenberg showed that an artificial mRNA made only of uracil (poly-U) produced a polypeptide made only of phenylalanine. This showed that the codon for phenylalanine is:
x: A chain of only uracil can contain only the codon UUU, so the phenylalanine produced must be coded by UUU. This was the first codon to be deciphered.

q: The coding (non-template) strand of a gene reads 5′-ATGGCA-3′. The mRNA made from this gene reads:
x: mRNA is complementary to the template strand, so it has the same sequence as the coding strand except that uracil replaces thymine.
